message.content: Lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) belong to two very different mammalian orders—Carnivora and Perissodactyla, respectively. Their most recent common ancestor is a placental mammal that lived during the late Paleocene to early Eocene (about 55–60 million years ago). This ancestor was part of the clade **Laurasiatheria**, the group that gave rise to many modern land mammals, including the lineages that eventually split into the orders Carnivora (big cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and Perissodactyla (horses, rhinos, tapirs, zebras, etc.). In other words, the lion and zebra share a common ancestor that was a basal Laurasiatherian mammal, predating the divergence of the carnivore and odd‑toed ungulate lineages.
